title: Your city. Your voice. Your vote on October 26.
content: The 2026 municipal and school board election is your opportunity to help shape the future of Kitchener. The decisions made by local elected officials affect everyday services, including roads, parks, community programs, Kitchener Fire Department, property taxes and more.
Take a few minutes today to make sure you're ready to vote on October 26, 2026.

You must be a Canadian citizen, at least 18 years old on October 26, 2026, and live in Kitchener, own or rent property in Kitchener, or be the spouse of an owner or tenant. Eligible voters must also not be prohibited from voting.
Check that you're on the voter list and that your name, address and school board information are up to date.

If you need to update your information, you can do this at City Hall, or you can also update your voter information at a voting location during advance voting or on Election Day. Allow extra time if you choose to amend/add yourself to the voters list when you go to vote..
Not on the voters list? You can still vote if you're eligible. Bring identification showing your name and current address.
Review the list of candidates and do your research to learn where they stand on the issues that matter most to you.
The City of Kitchener is providing a range of vote opportunities to remove barriers for residents so they can practice their democratic rights safely and easily.
The City is committed to making​​ voting accessible for everyone.

During Advance voting, Kitchener voters can “vote anywhere” at a number of facilities across the city including two Shop and Vote locations, the Kitchener Market and Fairview Park Mall. We’re taking the vote to where people are.

On voting day we provide accessible voting locations in every​ ward, offer different voting options and supply accessibility tools at voting locations. Voters may also bring their own devices to help mark their ballot. Learn more below about how we make voting accessible during municipal elections.
Kitchener voters looking for a convenient and accessible new voting method are encouraged to try drive thru voting.

Kitchener voters will remain in their vehicles until prompted to drive into the tent location. After turning off their vehicles, an election official will conduct the voting service at the vehicle window(s). Electors will be given a ballot in a privacy screen so that other people that may be in the vehicle cannot see their selections. Marked ballots will be collected back through the window(s) and cast into the tabulator. Once cast, the vehicle will exit the tent location.
Drive thru voting operates like the COVID-vaccination drive thru process.

It’s a convenient method for electors that may have mobility challenges, limits exposure for individuals who may have health considerations, and reduces the need to unbuckle and remove young children and seniors.
The dates and times that drive thru is being offered can be found on the Where to vote page .

Kitchener voters who cannot leave their homes due to illness, injury or disability may request a home vote visit where election workers will bring a ballot to them. The voter's caregiver(s) who are eligible voters may also vote during the home visit. Home votes will only take place within the boundaries of the City of Kitchener.

Home voting will be available for a limited number of appointments, between 9:30 a.m. and 3:30 p.m. on weekdays from Thursday, October 8 until Tuesday, October 20 (not including Thanksgiving, Monday, October 12).
Requests for home visits will be accepted starting on September 28.
You can request a home visit by;
email at election@kitchener.ca .
Voters are encouraged to book their own appointment as soon as possible.
The deadline to request a home voting appointment is at 4:30 p.m. on Monday, October 19, 2026.

If Kitchener voters are away for all the Advance Voting or Voting Day locations, they may appoint another eligible voter as a proxy to vote on their behalf.  To appoint a voting proxy, the voter and their proxy must complete two copies with original signatures of the Appointment for Voting Proxy form.

The voter being appointed as a proxy must then book an appointment at Kitchener City Hall. They must bring with them the two completed forms, their own ID, and a copy of ID for the voter who is appointing them that proves the voter’s residency and signature.

Voters requiring assistance can take advantage of a number of accessibility enhancements including; accessible ballot marking devices at advance and designated election day locations, magnifying sheets, translation through the city’s multi-language service interpretation service and support from service animals and support persons.
View the City’s Election Accessibility Plan for more details including other initiatives designed to make elections accessible.
Visit KitchenerVotes.ca for everything you need to know about voter eligibility, candidate information, voting options and locations and accessibility planning.
Make your mark. Local matters.

title: City of Kitchener celebrates grand reopening of Meadowlane Park and new stormwater management pond
content: Kitchener, ON - The City of Kitchener celebrated the completion and grand reopening of the Meadowlane Park and a new stormwater management pond on Saturday, marking a significant investment in climate resilience, environmental stewardship and community infrastructure.

Meadowlane Park has been transformed through a project designed to reduce flood risk, enhance water quality and strengthen climate resilience within the Sandrock Creek watershed and downstream neighbourhoods.

The project was identified through the City of Kitchener’s 2016 Integrated Stormwater Master Plan as an opportunity to improve stormwater management while enhancing green space. The new pond will help manage stormwater runoff before it enters local waterways, reducing impacts on the environment and supporting the community’s long-term resilience to more frequent and intense storms.

The project was supported through funding from all orders of government, including $2.143 million from the Government of Canada’s Disaster Mitigation and Adaptation Fund, $3 million from the Province of Ontario through the Building Faster Fund, and $178,500 from the Federation of Canadian Municipalities through the Growing Canada’s Community Canopies program , alongside contributions from the City of Kitchener.

“This project demonstrates the power of partnership. Meadowlane Park is a great example of what can be accomplished when all orders of government work together to invest in communities,” said Mayor Berry Vrbanovic. “On behalf of the City of Kitchener, I want to thank the Government of Canada, the Province of Ontario and the Federation of Canadian Municipalities for their support in bringing this important project to life. Together, we’re creating greener, more resilient public spaces that will benefit residents today and for generations to come.”

“Meadowlane Park has always been an important gathering place for residents in the Forest Heights neighbourhood, and I’m proud to see it transformed in a way that preserves its community character while delivering significant environmental benefits,” said Bil Ioannidis, Ward 7 Councillor. “This project reflects the feedback we heard from residents and demonstrates how community priorities and environmental stewardship can come together to create a stronger, more resilient neighbourhood.”

The project reflects extensive community engagement. Several residents volunteered significant time as members of the Meadowlane Park Community Resource Group, playing an active role in shaping both the engagement process and park design. Their contributions, alongside feedback gathered through six community engagement events, helped inform the final design and preserve valued community features while meeting the project's environmental and infrastructure objectives.

In addition to improving stormwater management, the project includes environmental enhancements that support a healthier and more resilient urban ecosystem, including new trees and naturalized areas supported through funding from the Federation of Canadian Municipalities’ Growing Canada’s Community Canopies program, as well as upgraded trails, new pond-side pathways and seating areas for residents to enjoy.
Quotes:

“By investing in stormwater management infrastructure, like Kitchener’s new stormwater management pond, the Government of Canada is taking action to better protect Canadians from the impacts of severe weather events and storms. The stormwater management pond will reduce the risk of flooding in streets and neighbourhoods near Meadowlane Park.”

– Tim Louis, Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the King’s Privy Council for Canada and Minister responsible for Canada-U.S. Trade, Intergovernmental Affairs, Internal Trade and One Canadian Economy and Member of Parliament for Kitchener—Conestoga

“Our government is proud to support partners like the City of Kitchener with the tools they need to make infrastructure investments that keep them strong, resilient, and ready for the future. Through the Building Faster Fund, we’re pleased to see municipalities deliver projects like Meadowlane Park that protect neighbourhoods from extreme weather, strengthen local infrastructure, and create vibrant public spaces for families to enjoy for years to come.”
– Rob Flack, Ontario’s Minister of Municipal Affairs and Housing.

“FCM is proud to support the City of Kitchener’s transformative tree-planting project. Through the Growing Canada’s Community Canopies initiative and with the support of the Government of Canada, we’re helping municipalities of every size get the right trees in the ground in the right places, creating cooler streets, cleaner air, and healthier neighbourhoods for decades to come.”
– Tim Tierney, President, Federation of Canadian Municipalities
About FCM’s Green Municipal Fund

FCM’s Green Municipal Fund (GMF) is a globally unique organization providing funding and education to municipalities to help them both reach net-zero and build resilient communities, while also delivering economic and social benefits such as jobs, housing and infrastructure. Since inception in 2000, it has helped reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 3.02 million tonnes, funded nearly 60,000 person-years of employment and contributed $5.6 billion to the national GDP via the more than 2,850 approved projects. GMF manages approximately $2.4 billion in programs funded by the Government of Canada.

The Green Municipal Fund’s Growing Canada’s Community Canopies is a $291M initiative, ending in 2031, funded by the Government of Canada and delivered by the FCM. Capacity building is enabled through a partnership with Tree Canada.

title: City of Kitchener invites community to share local stories as they put a Spotlight on Sport at the Cowan Recreation Centre
content: The City of Kitchener is inviting residents to help put a spotlight on local sports by celebrating the people and organizations who make Kitchener a vibrant, active and connected community through a permanent community showcase in the Cowan Recreation Centre at RBJ Schlegel Park.

When the facility opens on November 14, visitors will discover Spotlight on Sport , a community storytelling space located in the main corridor beside the Cowan Fieldhouse. Featuring four large digital displays, photos, memorabilia, athlete and team profiles, and rotating community-submitted stories, Spotlight on Sport will celebrate the athletes, coaches, officials, volunteers, teams, organizations, and community champions who have helped shape sport and recreation in Kitchener. Through featured profiles and community submissions, the exhibit showcases achievements, inspires participation, and highlights the many ways sport helps communities connect.

"Sport is about much more than competition. It creates connections, builds confidence, brings people together in what often become lifelong friendships, and helps create a sense of belonging in our community," said Mayor Berry Vrbanovic. "Every day, athletes, coaches, volunteers, officials, and organizations across Kitchener make a positive difference in the lives of others, here in Kitchener and often beyond our community’s borders. The Spotlight on Sport at the Cowan Recreation Centre gives us an opportunity to celebrate their contributions, preserve their stories, and inspire future generations to get involved."

From grassroots programs and neighbourhood leagues to provincial, national, and international achievements, Spotlight on Sport will showcase the many ways sport strengthens our community and creates meaningful connections. The exhibit will celebrate not only athletic success, but also leadership, inclusion, mentorship, volunteerism, and community building. The inaugural exhibit will feature Kitchener-born soccer players, Leticia Skeete and Markus Cimermancic, as well as former professional volleyball player Sarah Pavan and national men’s wheelchair basketball veteran, Tyler Miller.

"Every community has inspiring sport stories that deserve to be told," said Mark McGinley, Manager, Cowan Recreation Centre. "Whether it's a volunteer who has dedicated decades to local programs, a team that brought a community together, or a young athlete who inspires others through their commitment and determination, Spotlight on Sport will help share and celebrate those stories."

Do you know someone who is making a difference through sport in Kitchener? Share your stories or nominate an individual, team, or organization whose dedication, leadership, and accomplishments deserve recognition.
Learn more about Spotlight on Sport and submit a story or nomination at Kitchener.ca/spotlightonsport

title: Statement From Mayor Berry Vrbanovic: National Day for Truth & Reconciliation
content: Today, as we observe the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation, also known as Orange Shirt Day, we remember the children who were taken from their families and never returned home, and we honour the Survivors, their families and communities who continue to live with the impacts of the Residential School System.

The orange shirt we wear today comes from the story of Phyllis Webstad. She was six years old when the new orange shirt her grandmother bought her was taken away on her first day at residential school. Her story reminds us of the thousands of children who were taken from their families, and of those who never came home.
This is a day for remembrance, but it cannot end there.

Reconciliation is slow work. It asks us to sit with truths about this country that many of us were never taught, to challenge what we thought we knew, and to keep listening even when what we hear is difficult.

The impacts of residential schools and colonialism are not confined to history. They continue to be felt by Survivors, families and Indigenous communities today. That is why truth must remain at the heart of reconciliation, and why our responsibility to listen and learn continues long after September 30.

Here in Kitchener, the City has a responsibility to keep learning, to build meaningful relationships with Indigenous communities and to make space for Indigenous voices to help guide this work. That responsibility reaches into the decisions we make about our programs, services and public spaces, and into how we build relationships with First Nations, Inuit and Métis Peoples.

Each of us has a role as well. Take time to learn about the history and ongoing impacts of residential schools. Listen to the experiences and perspectives of Indigenous Peoples. Seek out Indigenous-led opportunities for learning and remembrance, and consider what reconciliation asks of you beyond today. The 2026 regional learning kit similarly calls on non-Indigenous people to take responsibility for our own learning and describes reconciliation as a year-round process.
Reconciliation requires more than a single day of reflection. What matters is what we carry forward from it, in what we learn, in the relationships we build, and in the choices we make.

Today, on behalf of Kitchener City Council, I encourage our community to remember the children who never came home, honour Survivors, their families and communities, and reflect on the responsibility each of us carries on the path toward reconciliation.
Berry Vrbanovic, on behalf of Kitchener City Council

title: Compass Kitchener report card highlights strong progress on City’s strategic priorities
content: Kitchener, ON – Compass Kitchener, a resident advisory committee, has released its 2025 Report Card reviewing the City of Kitchener's progress on its strategic priorities. For the third consecutive year, Compass Kitchener's Report Card finds that all projects evaluated under the 2023-2026 Strategic Plan either met or exceeded expectations.
The twelve 2025 projects included in this review advanced the City's priorities on housing, transportation, sustainability, economic development and community wellbeing.

“This report card reflects the significant progress we've made on the priorities that matter most to our community during this term of Council," said Mayor Berry Vrbanovic. "Whether it's creating more housing options, investing in safer transportation networks, growing our tree canopy or enhancing public spaces, the Strategic Plan continues to guide investments that improve quality of life for residents while also always focusing on affordability. I want to thank Compass Kitchener for their long-standing independent perspective, which helps ensure both Council and staff remain focused on achieving our strategic goals and realizing our shared vision for Kitchener’s future."

Compass Kitchener is one of the only resident-led committees in municipalities across Canada that is dedicated to supporting the development of the strategic plan, evaluating its outcomes and reporting directly to Council.

The committee evaluates completed projects based on responsible delivery, public value, transparency, communication and community engagement. Its work gives Council and residents an additional measure of accountability and insight into the City’s progress on its strategic priorities.

“ It’s an honour to serve as Chair of Compass Kitchener and help provide Council with an independent community perspective on the City’s Strategic Plan,” said Troy Glover, Chair of Compass Kitchener. “As members, we help shape the City’s community engagement approach for each strategic planning cycle, support key community engagement activities, ensure community perspectives are accurately reflected by providing feedback to staff, and evaluate the City’s progress on strategic priorities once the plan has been approved by Council.”
Residents can read the Compass Kitchener report here.

“I’m incredibly proud of the work City staff are doing to bring Kitchener’s Strategic Plan to life. The progress being made in our community reflects the dedication, innovation, and collaboration across the organization ," said Dan Chapman, Chief Administrative Officer. “It’s encouraging to see residents recognize and take pride in these accomplishments, and I value Compass Kitchener’s independent review of our progress. Their perspective helps ensure we stay accountable to the goals we’ve set and continue moving closer to our shared 20-year vision for Kitchener.”

Work has been underway since January to develop Kitchener's 2027-2030 Strategic Plan. Since we have started, over 1,500 residents have helped shape future priorities through surveys, community conversations and other engagement activities across the city. Residents can follow the Strategic Plan process and upcoming milestones at engagewr.ca/KitchenerStrategicPlan .

title: Key Decisions of Kitchener Council: September 28, 2026
content: Key Decisions of Council is a summary of major discussion items presented at Kitchener City Council meetings. It is circulated following each meeting. Please refer to the minutes for an official record of the meeting.
The City of Kitchener has launched a new action plan to support local businesses, protect jobs, and respond to ongoing tariff and trade uncertainty.

Kitchener's Action Plan to Support Local and Protect Jobs includes five key areas of action: using City spending to support Ontario and Canadian suppliers, making it easier for residents to choose local, helping businesses adapt and grow, advocating for Kitchener’s business and workforce needs, and opening new markets and attracting investment.
The City is also encouraging residents to support Kitchener businesses and choose Canadian-made products whenever possible.
Residents and businesses can learn more about the action plan, available supports and ways to choose local at Kitchener.ca/SupportLocal .

Kitchener City Council recognized 11 affiliated neighbourhood associations and minor sports organizations for their long-standing contributions to the community through the annual Long Service Awards. This year’s recipients represent a combined 435 years of service, including milestone anniversaries ranging from five to 65 years. The awards recognize the dedication of volunteers who help build strong neighbourhoods and support recreation and sport opportunities across the city.
Recipients included:
Auditorium Neighbourhood Association (35 years)
Doon Pioneer Park Community Association (45 years)
Eastwood Neighbourhood Association (5 years)
Mill-Courtland Neighbourhood Association (40 years)
Conestoga Sailing Club (65 years)
Kitchener Minor Girls Softball Association (60 years)
Kitchener-Waterloo Water Polo Club (50 years)
Region of Waterloo Swim Club (50 years)
Top Spin Table Tennis Club of KW (25 years)
Tsuruoka Kai Karate Do KW (30 years)
Waterloo Region Minor Football Association (30 years)

Council received Compass Kitchener’s report card evaluating 12 completed actions from the City’s 2023-2026 Strategic Plan. For more than 20 years, the Compass Kitchener Advisory Committee has worked with the City to evaluate progress on actions identified through the Strategic Plan.

Using its standardized evaluation framework, the committee found that all 12 actions evaluated met or exceeded expectations. Four projects were rated Exceeds Expectations, and eight were rated Meets Expectations, with no projects receiving a Does Not Meet Expectations rating.
The results reflect continued progress in delivering the actions identified in the 2023-2026 Strategic Plan and provide Council with an independent assessment of the City’s progress.
To learn more, read the report here .

title: Kitchener launches action plan to support local businesses and protect jobs
content: The City of Kitchener has launched a new action plan to support local businesses, protect jobs and help the community respond to ongoing tariff and trade uncertainty.

Kitchener’s Plan to Support Local and Protect Jobs focuses on five key areas of action: supporting local and Canadian businesses through City spending, making it easier to choose local, helping businesses adapt and grow, turning local evidence into advocacy and action and opening new markets and attracting investment. The plan reflects Kitchener’s strengths in advanced manufacturing, technology, healthcare and exports, as well as the exposure of those sectors to changing trade conditions, North American supply chains and U.S. tariffs.

“We can’t resolve an international trade dispute from Kitchener City Hall, but we’re not powerless. In fact, we believe some of the most meaningful work is being done right here at home,” said Mayor Berry Vrbanovic. “This plan puts the tools we have to work. We’ll use City spending more deliberately, make it easier for residents to choose local, help businesses access practical support and ensure Kitchener’s voice is heard by provincial, federal, and international decision-makers. Behind every economic statistic is a person wondering whether their job is secure or whether their business can absorb another increase in costs. They deserve a City that pays attention and acts where it can.”
The plan includes five key areas of action:

1. Put City spending to work for local businesses The City will continue to prioritize eligible Ontario and Canadian suppliers, look for practical Canadian alternatives to U.S.-supplied goods and create more opportunities for local businesses to compete for City contracts. Approximately 98 per cent of the City’s current spending on goods, services and construction already goes to Ontario-based businesses.

2. Make it easier to choose local The City will build Support Local into a year-round effort that helps residents, organizations and businesses find products, services and experiences made in Kitchener. This work will include business features, community partnerships, local markets, pop-ups and supplier showcases.

3. Help businesses adapt, diversity, and grow The City will work directly with businesses in manufacturing, technology, healthcare and other trade-exposed sectors to connect them with funding opportunities, investment, and growth supports. Through direct consultations, a central online resource, practical advice, workshops and referrals, businesses will be better equipped to identify Canadian alternatives, strengthen supply chains, pursue new markets and adapt to changing economic conditions. The City will also monitor local economic impacts to help guide future action.

4. Turn local evidence into advocacy and action The City will meet directly with businesses facing the greatest trade-related risks, identify gaps in existing programs and advocate for solutions that respond to Kitchener’s business and workforce needs. This will include working through municipal associations and with Canadian and U.S. partners to communicate the local impacts of tariffs.

5. Open new market and attract investments The City will use its convening power, partnerships and international relationships to bring buyers, investors and new business opportunities directly to Kitchener companies and to position the city as a competitive place to invest and grow.  We’re starting with two events next month, co-hosted with Senator Sandra Pupatello. The Canada Buys and Defence Shift sessions on October 13 and 14, will connect Kitchener businesses directly with federal and provincial procurement decisionmakers, prime contractors and tier-one suppliers in the defence sector.

The action plan builds on the work of Kitchener’s Tariff and Trade Task Force and the City’s ongoing collaboration with businesses, industry associations, economic development organizations and other levels of government.
We are also encouraging residents to choose Kitchener businesses and Canadian-made products whenever possible, explore neighbourhood restaurants and retailers and share local business stories.

Choosing local is not the only answer to global trade uncertainty but it is one direct way residents can support local jobs and the people who have invested in Kitchener. Every purchase builds Kitchener.
Residents and businesses can learn more about the action plan, available supports and ways to choose local at Kitchener.ca/SupportLocal .

title: Kitchener Fire Department: Major incident report – September 27, 2026
content: At approximately 8:00 a.m., Kitchener Fire crews responded to a reported structure fire at a detached residential dwelling on Village Road. Upon arrival, crews encountered a fire that had extended into the attic space of the home and worked quickly to bring the incident under control.
The fire caused significant structural damage to the residence, resulting in the displacement of the occupants. Damage is currently estimated between $500,000 and $750,000.
There were no reported injuries to civilians or firefighters, and the fire is not considered suspicious.

title: Club 51 Sports Bar scores big with fans during Kitchener Rangers home opener
content: Kitchener, ON – Hundreds of hockey fans got their first game-day experience at Club 51 Sports Bar during the Kitchener Rangers' home opener last Friday, marking a strong start for the new sports bar and gathering space at the Kitchener Memorial Auditorium (The Aud).

The successful opening followed a sneak peek celebration held earlier in the week, where members of the media, City council, staff, project partners and construction teams gathered for a ribbon cutting and first look at the transformed space. The event recognized the work that went into converting the former Subscribers Lounge into a modern restaurant and community gathering place inside The Aud.

"For 75 years, The Aud has been one of Kitchener's most beloved gathering places," said Mayor Berry Vrbanovic. “In May 2025, our Council approved $2M to bring in a vibrant dining space for concert goers, sports fans and residents. I'm proud of the innovative projects we’ve taken on, like Club 51, that show how thoughtful investments can honour a facility’s history while creating new experiences that meet the needs of today's residents and visitors.”
Hometown hospitality

Designed to serve guests year-round, Club 51 offers elevated pub fare, local craft beverages and a strong focus on supporting local suppliers and producers throughout Waterloo Region. In addition to game-day offerings, Club 51 will welcome fans in for Rangers’ away game streaming and other event opportunities.

Matt and Jackie Rolleman, owners and operators of Club 51 Sports Bar, said the vision was to create a welcoming destination that reflects the energy and history of The Aud while delivering a premium hospitality experience.

"Seeing the restaurant come to life during the Rangers' home opener was incredibly rewarding," said Jackie Rolleman, co-owner of Club 51. "We were proud to welcome so many people from across the community. Fans arrived early, families stayed for dinner and people took the time to enjoy the space. The turnout showed us just how much people value having another place to gather at The Aud."
For reservations, menus and operating hours, visit Club 51 Sports Bar's website . Find tickets for games, events and concerts at The Aud on KitchenerLIVE.ca .
About The Aud

Since opening in 1951, The Aud has served as one of Kitchener's premier entertainment and community venues, hosting sporting events, concerts, exhibitions, family programming and community celebrations. In 2026, The Aud celebrates its 75th anniversary.
About Club 51 Sports Bar

Owned and operated by The Rolleman Group, Club 51 Sports Bar is a modern take on the classic sports bar, proudly located inside the historic Kitchener Memorial Auditorium. Named after the year The Aud opened in 1951, Club 51 blends the rich history of this iconic venue with elevated pub fare, local craft beer, Ontario-made beverages, and warm hospitality.
Club 51 Sports Bar proudly continues the tradition of bringing community and sport together in one place.
For more information:  Corporate Communications and Marketing City of Kitchener media@kitchener.ca

title: King StrEATery Food Truck Festival highlights 50 local businesses in Downtown Kitchener this Sunday
content: Kitchener is celebrating local businesses, entrepreneurs and artisans with the re-launch of Downtown Kitchener's popular King StrEATery Food Truck Festival this Sunday, September 27 from 11 a.m. to 7 p.m. on King Street East (from Eby to Cedar Street), at the Kitchener Market piazza and many east end businesses.

King StrEATery, a vibrant, pedestrian-friendly celebration, will bring together 50 participating local businesses, including 15 food trucks, as well as food vendors, east end shops and cafes, and a Love Local Artisan Market for a day of food, shopping and community in the heart of downtown.
Browse one-of-a-kind goods at the Love Local Artisan Market featuring more than 15 local entrepreneurs and artisans and explore the shops and businesses of Kitchener’s east end.

Along with great food and shopping, visitors can enjoy Drew Ripley’s Big Balloon Show, buskers, giant games, free dance lessons (K-Pop, salsa and line dancing with TenC Dance Co.) and relax in the licensed outdoor bar area.

Admission is free, and free Sunday parking is available, including at the Kitchener Market parking garage. Visitors are also encouraged to bring a non-perishable food donation for The Food Bank of Waterloo Region .
For the full list of food trucks, food vendors, Love Local Artisan Market and participating east end businesses, visit DowntownKitchener.ca/KingStreatery.
